title: Client BFF stream heuristics and tool telemetry PRD (sketch)
body:
Context
We increasingly see customers build a lightweight ‘client BFF’ (backend-for-frontend) adjacent to their frontend to hide auth, fan-out tool calls, and adapt a single client surface to different device constraints. This PRD sketches a hosted-API oriented design: documented heuristics for when the client-BFF should buffer, prefetch, or proxy streaming frames; a compact tool-calling contract that supports progressive responses; and a telemetry schema so we can reason about latency/cost tradeoffs at the per-route level.

Problem statement
- Customers implementing streaming endpoints often duplicate brittle buffering and reassembly logic in each BFF.
- Tool-calling orchestration is split: the Hosted API may want to return partial structured results while the BFF also needs to call external tools (search, DB) deterministically.
- Observability is fragmented: telemetry from the client, BFF, and Redwood-hosted endpoint are not stitched, making it hard to quantify the unit economics of streaming + tool orchestration.

Goals
- Provide a recommended BFF streaming handshake that minimizes duplicate code and edge-case bugs (resume, fragment loss, client reconnect).
- Define a small, robust tool-call envelope that preserves incremental outputs while allowing BFF-mediated tool hedging and fallbacks.
- Ship a telemetry event model and sampling guidance enabling per-request latency/cost attribution (client -> BFF -> Hosted API -> tool).

Non-goals
- Replacing customer BFFs or prescribing specific backend languages.
- Reworking the core streaming protocol (this is compatibility-focused; we add optional envelopes and fields).

Success metrics (first 90 days after rollout)
- 30% reduction in BFF-side incident reports related to streaming reconnects or partial-response reassembly for customers using the pattern.
- Telemetry coverage: >= 60% of new streaming routes emit the recommended telemetry events.
- Pilot customers (2–3) adopt the tool-call envelope and report fewer mismatches between tool outputs and final structured responses.

User stories
- Frontend engineer: "I want my mobile app to receive progressive results for a large generation while keeping the socket connection cheap and resilient to flaky networks."
- BFF owner: "I want a simple library that decodes frames, resumes gaps reliably, and lets me orchestrate tool calls without losing partial results."
- Platform engineer: "I want telemetry that ties a token count spike to a specific tool call pattern so we can suggest batching/quantization improvements."

Proposed high-level design
1) BFF handshake and frame semantics (backwards compatible)
- Optional header: X-Redwood-BFF-Mode: resume|proxy|buffered. Suggest default = resume.
- Resume: BFF stores incremental checkpoints (client-visible sequence id + checksum). On reconnect, client resends last ack id; Hosted API replays from that point.
- Proxy: BFF streams frames through without modification (low-latency pass-through). Best for trusted internal networks.
- Buffered: BFF aggregates small frames for clients with high jitter to reduce chattiness and rate charges. Buffering heuristic: if median inter-frame gap < 50ms for 1s, buffer up to 200ms or until top-level semantic boundary emitted.

2) Tool-call envelope (compact, progressive-friendly)
- tool_call_start: { id, requested_tools, hint: {blocking:true|false}, client_metadata } (encoded as small JSON per frame)
- tool_call_progress: frames that carry partial tool outputs (structured fragments) with sequence ids that can be merged by the BFF.
- tool_call_end: final status (success|error|fallback) and canonical output pointer (if offloaded to object store).
- Key properties: idempotency token, small deterministic merge semantics (append or replace per field), and an escape hatch where the Hosted API can mark a fragment as provisional so BFF can surface to client but still attempt a fallback.

3) Structured output envelope and schema contracts
- Enforce a top-level envelope: {version, session_id, fragment_id, content_type, body, hints} where content_type is e.g., text/plain, application/json+rdw (Redwood-typed).
- Body may be partial; fragments include a reconciliation policy: merge_strategy: {append_lines, replace_field, merge_map_by_key}. BFFs should implement a minimal merge utility shipped as an SDK helper.

4) SDK ergonomics (BFF-side helpers)
- Provide small middleware for common BFF frameworks (Express/Koa, FastAPI, Node+Cloud Functions) that:
  - parses stream frames and reassembles structured fragments
  - exposes a simple API: onFragment(fragment) => optional toolCalls to make; emitClient(fragment) to forward progressive results to client
  - helper to sign and validate resume tokens and checksums
- Idiomatic surface: sync-looking handler that yields partial responses (async iter) to make developer migration simple.

5) Telemetry model
- Events (all optional but recommended):
  - rdw.client.connect (client metadata, network tier)
  - rdw.bff.frame.received (frame_id, size_bytes, seq_id, resume_token_present)
  - rdw.bff.tool.call (tool_id, blocking_hint, latency_ms, success)
  - rdw.hosted.stream.frame (seq_id, tokens_generated, model_variant)
  - rdw.hosted.tool.hedge (tool_id, fallback_used, tokens_delta)
  - rdw.bff.client.forwarded (client_latency_ms, frames_forwarded_count)
- Sampling guidance: high-volume frames -> reservoir sample 1% but always capture the first N frames and any error frames. Ensure linked trace_id is present to stitch across BFF and Hosted logs.

Operational considerations and rollout path
- Phase 0: publish RFC + SDK helpers as alpha; do not change existing protocol defaults.
- Phase 1: add optional headers and envelope parsing in SDK; offer CLI tool to replay/resume sessions for debugging. Pilot with 2 internal teams + 1 external customer.
- Phase 2: promote SDK to stable, add telemetry ingestion parsers in Console for visualizing BFF->Hosted traces and token cost breakdowns.

Compatibility and safety tradeoffs
- Backwards compatibility: frames without our envelope should be treated as opaque text frames. Our middleware must gracefully ignore unknown content_type values.
- Security: resume tokens are HMAC-signed with a short TTL; BFFs must not persist unencrypted tokens beyond TTL. Avoid putting PII in fragment hints.

Open questions / decisions needing product/infra
- How large should the default buffered window be for mobile UIs? (200ms is an initial heuristic, collect metrics to iterate)
- Should we surface a standard BFF-side SDK metric that maps directly to Console billing dashboards? (recommended: yes)
- Are we comfortable exposing tool-call partial outputs to clients before the final reconciliation? (product risk: potential confusion; mitigations: provisional flag + UI guidance)

Next steps (owner: Sofia)
- Share RFC with eng-serving-runtime and devexp for SDK feasibility (week 1).
- Implement Express/FastAPI middleware prototypes and a small e2e demo (week 2–3).
- Add telemetry ingestion spike parser in Console prototype (week 4).

Notes to reviewers
- This doc assumes low-impact protocol additions only. If runtime changes are needed (e.g., server-side prefix checkpointing), we will follow a separate infra design doc.
- Ask: signal review on the resume-token format and whether the buffering heuristic sounds reasonable for our initial mobile-focused pilot.
